newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak reforms depend on more investment - banker.
newsitem.headline: Slovak reforms depend on more investment - banker.

text.p: Slovakia must attract more foreign investment to complete its post-Communist reforms, Wolfgang Roth, vice-president of the European Investment Bank (EIB), said on Tuesday.
Roth said politicians needed to do a better job at selling Slovakia abroad and stop bickering.

"The strategic issue for the next two to three years is that the Slovak government manages to get the direct investment for its industry," he told a conference of bankers and business leaders in Banska Bystrica, central Slovakia.
"Only direct foreign investment can ensure further economic development," he declared.

Political infighting between Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar and President Michal Kovac, and between Meciar's government and opposition politicians has caused analysts to question the stability of the investment environment in the Slovakia.

Foreign direct investment (FDI) in Slovakia totalled only $808.4 million between January 1990 and June 1996 while neighbouring Hungary has attracted some $11 billion and former federation partner, the Czech Republic, over $5.0 billion.
Roth said the EIB was ready to increase its capital in Slovakia, currently standing at some 500 million marks.
"If we (EIB) are given good projects, we can even double our investment in Slovakia," Roth said.
He added the bank could provide money within 10 months, and that the main areas of interest were the transport sector as well as restructuring of the bank loan portfolios.
Roth warned that there could appear certain concerns over the worsening Slovak trade balance, if FDI fails to compensate for the growing deficit.
He called for speeding up the pace of the country's economic reforms to match other EU aspirants.
"Slovakia has to restructure its economy. It is already time to catch up with other European Union (EU) candidates," he said.

"Strangely enough, inflation and growth development in Slovakia are better than in those countries, so then it appears that Slovak politicians have to ask the question why their country's attraction is lower," he added. -- Tatiana Vacova, Bratislava Newsroom, 42-7-21-3687
